headlines.summary: A Microsoft outage on Thursday affected users of services like Outlook, Teams and 365.
headlines.article_text: Microsoft outage continues, Outlook and other 365 services down Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points A Microsoft outage on Thursday and Friday affected users of services like Outlook, Teams and 365. The company said it did not suspect malicious activity was the cause and it was attempting to restore operations. Amazon Web Services said it was "operating normally" and noted inaccurate reports of outages on its platforms. In this article MSFT Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 2:27 02:27 Microsoft outage hits hundreds of millions, CNBC anchors can't read your emails Squawk Box Europe Microsoft suffered a widespread outage on Thursday and Friday, as engineers scrambled to fix server issues that caused disruption to millions of its customers. Connectivity issues began shortly before 1 p.m. ET on Thursday and continued into Friday, with Outlook and Teams, along with multiple Microsoft 365 services such as Sharepoint and Copilot, affected. Numerous external services that connect with Microsoft products such as Outlook Calendar were also hit. 'Early signs of stabilization' A sign on the Microsoft campus in Redmond, Washington, US, Oct. 26, 2026. David Ryder | Reuters Microsoft said it was not aware of any malicious activity causing the outage, which it initially blamed on a traffic surge in part of its infrastructure and issues with a component responsible for processing server health. Email and related tools were unavailable for Microsoft users throughout the Asian business day on Friday and across the European and early U.S. morning. In an update at around 6 a.m. ET, Microsoft said users may still be unable to connect to multiple Microsoft 365 products — including Outlook on either web or desktop and any services that interact with email — and did not give a timeline for restoring full service. Most access to Teams was available. The company said recovery actions were complete across some affected infrastructure in the Asia Pacific region, where service was being "gradually restored," and some users were getting access to their inboxes. Microsoft is focused on extending the recovery actions to affected infrastructure in other regions and adding capacity to improve service, it added. Earlier in the day, Microsoft said its efforts were showing "early signs of stabilization," but significant numbers of users continued to experience issues. Engineering teams are taking affected systems offline for fixes and bringing them back online in stages. Microsoft said it is prioritizing efforts to preserve emails delayed during the recovery process and reduce email queues and backlogs. It is extending the timeout window, whereby delayed emails continue to attempt delivery, to 48 hours to help protect messages. The company said in its initial updates on Thursday that the connectivity problems related to infrastructure "elevated load across multiple regions," caused by a "number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure." Some servers were failing automated health checks, it said. Microsoft shares were around 2% lower in premarket trade. Governments and businesses review impact Governments and businesses in Asia-Pacific and Europe said they were monitoring the situation, which was causing widespread disruption. The U.K.'s National Health Service said the outage was affecting some of its services but that patients should attend appointments as normal. Calls "may be subject to long waits" as a result of disruption to the organization, a hospital group serving South West London and the English county of Surrey said on X. Earnings for Swiss luxury goods giant Richemont were slightly delayed on Friday due to the outage. Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on Nov. 12, rescheduled the release to Nov. 16, citing business disruptions caused by the global Microsoft outage. Air India said it had "temporarily rerouted" emails so it could continue to receive customer messages, adding that its flight operations were not affected. Australian Home Affairs and Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke said in a press conference that Microsoft "believe they are dealing in some ways similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry," Reuters reported. A fault with an update issued by cybersecurity company CrowdStrike caused one of the world's biggest IT system outages in 2024 , hitting airlines, banks and more, Microsoft reported in 2025 that Copilot, its collection of AI assistants and tools, had more than 100 million monthly active users. Amazon Web Services and Google users also reported outages on the site on Thursday. Amazon wrote on X that services were "operating normally" and an "unrelated disruption elsewhere on the internet is prompting some inaccurate news reports." The company referred users to its health dashboard for "accurate data." At 4 p.m. ET Thursday, Microsoft said it had "validated an alternative service health check method" that brought some affected servers back online. "We're now applying this change more broadly," Microsoft wrote. "We're also preparing automated recovery systems to continually detect and restart unresponsive servers, to maintain service stability while this change progresses." headlines.article_text: Canada to sue Stellantis as Trump trade war reshapes production plans Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Canada gave Stellantis 30 days to address alleged breaches of a federal funding agreement or face potential legal action. The dispute escalated after Stellantis signed an agreement to sell its idled Brampton assembly plant to Canadian defense manufacturer Roshel. A Stellantis executive said the company would return $24 million in federal support, while Ottawa says the automaker could owe hundreds of millions of dollars. In this article STLA Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Industry Minister Melanie Joly addresses media at Sheraton Center Toronto Hotel following sale of Stellantis, November 12, 2026. Sophie Bouquillon | Toronto Star | Getty Images Canada has threatened to sue auto giant Stellantis over the planned sale of an idled assembly plant in Brampton, Ontario, alleging breaches of a federal funding agreement after the carmaker announced plans to shift production to the U.S. amid President Donald Trump 's trade war. Speaking at a news conference on Thursday, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said the government had served Stellantis with a formal notice of default, giving the company 30 days to address its concerns or face legal action. "We sent a notice of default and, basically, they have 30 days — or else, of course, we will sue them," Joly told reporters in Toronto. Joly said Stellantis had violated its contractual commitments to the Canadian government and the workers at Brampton by announcing an agreement to sell the plant to armored vehicle manufacturer Roshel earlier in the week. She added that the company was now "on the hook" for hundreds of millions of dollars over the move. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has described the situation at the Brampton plant as "unacceptable" and a "betrayal" of its workers. A spokesperson for Stellantis, which owns auto brands including Jeep, Dodge, Fiat, Chrysler and Peugeot, was not immediately available to comment when contacted by CNBC on Friday morning. The standoff comes as the U.S. and Canada remain locked in a bitter trade dispute , with Trump repeatedly putting pressure on automakers to move vehicle production south of the border. Stellantis had scrapped plans to build its Jeep Compass at the Brampton plant and shifted future production to a factory in Illinois amid U.S. auto tariffs and other market pressures. New York-listed shares of Stellantis year-to-date. Stellantis Canada CEO Trevor Longley reportedly said Thursday that the company would return $24 million in federal subsidies after announcing plans to sell the Brampton plant, a figure that falls well below the government's estimate of what the company owes. "We recognize the disappointment and uncertainty surrounding the future of the facility. While our decision to sell the plant represents a change from the original plans for Brampton, the agreement we have advanced with a Canadian manufacturer provides a path to return the facility to productive industrial use," Longley said, according to CBC News . Jeep Grand Cherokee SUVs at a dealership in Mississauga, Ontario, Canada, on Friday, Oct. 17, 2025. Bloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty Images Stellantis said Monday that it had agreed to sell the Brampton assembly plant to Roshel for an undisclosed amount. It also acknowledged its obligations to employees at the facility and said it remains prepared to work with Unifor, Canada's largest private sector union, to negotiate a settlement to assist union-represented employees. Stellantis stock has fallen sharply since the start of the year, with its Milan-listed shares down more than 60% for 2026 so far.
